Question: After a long cross-country road trip, my dog growled and started a fight with another dog for the first time ever. Is this an isolated incident due to anxiety or should I take him to a behaviorist for his aggression?
Answer: OK, you tell me: Have you ever been worn-out tired, gotten angry, and started a fight? I know that I have. So, why should your dog be any different? Why should your dog be penalized because you — as his owner — failed to protect him? You chose not to act like a “parent” and shield your dog — from behavior that you should have anticipated. So, if you think your dog should be taken “to a behaviorist for his aggression” — then why shouldn’t you be taken “to a behaviorist” for failing to act responsibly? Don’t blame the dog. Look in the mirror.

Question: In your own opinion or view? What is the latest "2021" top best kind of dog food?
Answer: We believe in dry dog food, which we use as treats as well as food. Dry dog food — softened with warm tap water and with something nice on top (like canned puppy food or canned chicken or tuna, etc.) — works perfectly for pups/dogs of every age. “Made in China” is a serious negative, so for us this eliminates “Royal Canin” and many more: Dog Food Made in China – Controversy, Melamine, Risks, Brands & FAQs This is also why we do not ever feed our dogs any treats made by any manufacturer: Dogs have died from “treats” and pig ears and such. Skip all of this! Instead, give your pup pieces of apple, carrots, frozen green peas, cooked and sliced sweet potato, etc. (We also keep small containers of our dogs’ dry dog food available to use as “treats” — our dogs view these “kibbles” as special and delightful, while we view their kibbles as safe, easy to keep on hand, fresh, and totally trustworthy. For us, it’s win, win!) We start our pups on the same food that they will eat for the rest of their lives, simply moving from puppy to grown dog to senior, as their lives progress. We live in the USA, so we are able to feed our dogs Fromm’s Large Breed Puppy Gold Dog Food (a Wisconsin-made dog food by folks we trust). Fromm’s does not sell to places like PetSmart and other big box pet food stores, but is available at most good private pet stores and is shipped by Fromm’s to our house. (Our English mastiffs — pictured at the bottom of this answer — have been fed Fromm’s all their lives.) Two other brands that I have found to be both good-quality and readily available American brands are IAMS PROACTIVE HEALTH Smart Puppy Large Breed Dry Dog Food Chicken, 15 lb. Bag - Walmart.com and Purina ONE Natural Large Breed Dry Puppy Food, SmartBlend Formula, 16.5 lb. Bag - Walmart.com (FYI: Walmart’s “Old Roy” is not recommended.) Before we found Fromm’s, we have fed Iams and Purina: Both are long-standing brands here in this country, consequently I presume them to be trustworthy. (I have serious doubts about “designer dogs” and “designer dog foods”: Both to me seem to appeal more to one’s ego, than to reason and worth.) Of all the American brands, at the very top of my list is Fromm’s because I know I can trust these folks. I will never choose to feed my dogs anything else. If I lived in Europe or Asia, I would feed “Happy Dog” because of its long history of European manufacture: “From Wehringen (Grermany) to the world: We export our products to over 70 countries on 3 continents.” All you feed is love - it's the most important ingredient in our food These are our two English mastiffs: Trixie is 8, has a trim figure, a healthy body, and looks to have a long life ahead, while Shomer is still a puppy who will grow to weigh about 175-pounds (Trixie is about 150-pounds). Both have been fed Fromm’s. Both are thriving and happy, happy. Wishing you and your dog every joy!

Question: We’re purchasing a show potential male puppy from a breeder. We do not intend to show (or breed) the dog. The contract states she can use the puppy (once it’s of age) as a stud, with no remuneration to us. Is this typical?
Answer: Huh? Given that it is in a male dog’s best interest — both physically and emotionally — for the dog to be neutered, I’m left wondering if your question is prompted by your underlying worry about the breeder. Calling oneself a breeder and having a kennel does not make one honorable and reputable: Some “breeders” are as flakey as a coconut pie. It appears to me that this breeder seems to put the breeder’s interests far above any concern for you, the buyer. If this is “typical” of this breeder’s behavior with buyers, I wonder what happens to the pups…. Puppyhood is vitally important, so my standards for any breeder are demanding: I expect socialized, healthy, happy puppies who start the world with joy and adventure in their hearts. This is my question to you: Is your potential pup likely to feel safe, welcome and joyous because of the treatment the breeder has given? You are risking your heart… Wishing you and yours stay safe, happy and healthy, Leslie Isbell

Question: Can I take my dog to the vet without papers?
Answer: YES!!!! Your vet doesn’t care if your pup/dog has “papers” (as in AKC registration, etc.), The vet can issue the papers you really need: Proof of vaccinations and, especially, proof of Rabies shots, as well as registration with the county/parish (via the Rabies tag.) Put the rabies tag on your dog’s collar and keep your vet records together, available to take with you whenever you need them. If your pup/dog has AKC registration papers, you may want to frame them for fun or preserve them if you plan on showing your dog in an AKC show, etc. If you are like us, with no plans to breed your dog, AKC “papers” are only the written assurance that the dog is the breed you thought you were getting. Face it, once you have your pup/dog, only breeders and the AKC care about AKC papers. Love your pup/dog, check out the vets (Office clean? People nice? Reputation good?) and make an appointment to see your chosen vet! You and your pup/dog are the important ones here, you are hiring a vet to help you: So expect professionalism and good treatment!
